extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of stand-up comedy, and performers researching comedic style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for crafting and performing stand-up comedy that emphasizes observational, clean, self-deprecating, and physical humor aimed at broad/family-friendly audiences. Includes markers of style, subject matter, performance technique, and career-success indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational comedy (subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material typically covers everyday events and ordinary experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include shipping a package with UPS, mortgages, and visits to the optometrist — i.e., find humor in daily-life situations that many audience members recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean comedy (content restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances are often described as 'clean' — refraining from profanity and taboo subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid coarse language and topics likely to be considered taboo; rely on wit and relatable situations rather than shock or explicit content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of body language and facial expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Known for incorporating body language and facial expressions into the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical delivery and nonverbal cues are core tools — gestures, posture, and facial work should support and amplify the observational or self-deprecating material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses self-deprecating humor as a recurring element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often comes from exposing one's own foibles or awkwardness; frequent references to personal/chosen vulnerabilities (e.g., childhood memories) make material accessible and affectionate rather than mean-spirited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporates physical/comedic movement as a genre element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond facial expressions, use of physicality (movement, mime, exaggerated action) is an identified stylistic dimension — pair physical bits with observational premises for clarity and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent childhood and nostalgic references
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes frequent references to childhood experiences (little league, grade school spelling bees, science projects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tapping into universal childhood memories creates relatable material; such references can serve both observational and self-deprecating jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility across performance mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: Performs across stand-up, television, film, and streaming platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success is demonstrated by adapting material for different formats (live stand-up, TV talk shows, specials, sketch series, film cameos) — tailor pacing and visuals to the medium (e.g., tighter bits for TV, longer stories for live shows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Career and recognition markers as measures of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators of acclaim and professional standing include TV appearances (The Tonight Show, Letterman), Netflix specials, selling out nationwide tours, and praise from peer comedians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These milestones (specials, prominent guest spots, sold-out tours, peer endorsements) are presented as evidence of quality and industry recognition; aspiring performers can use similar benchmarks to gauge progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influences shaping comedic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites established comedians (Johnny Carson, Steve Martin, George Carlin, Richard Pryor, David Letterman) as influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding and referencing the techniques or personas of influential figures can contextualize stylistic choices — study these influences to inform timing, delivery, and thematic choices while developing an original voice.
